subtype: Stage 3: Confusion for the one ignored [Receiver]
passage: Nikita sat behind the counter of her father's kirana shop in Nashik district, weighing out sugar without looking at the scale. Gautam hadn't spoken to her in four days. Not at the bus stand, not at tuition, not even when she held out her mango to share like always. What had she done? She went through it again. Was it the joke about his cycle? Did he hear she'd topped the test? Was he angry she didn't come to his cousin's wedding? Between customers she scrolled back through their chats, three months of them, searching for the message that broke something. Nothing. If he'd shouted at her, at least she'd know. This quiet was worse. Her stomach hurt all evening.

qa.q: How many days had it been since Gautam spoke to Nikita?
qa.a: Gautam hadn't spoken to her in four days.

qa.q: Why does the silence feel worse to Nikita than shouting would?
qa.a: With shouting she would at least know what she did; the silence leaves her guessing and anxious, with her stomach hurting.

qa.q: What could Nikita do next instead of searching old chats?
qa.a: She could ask Gautam gently and directly, "I feel like something's wrong between us. Will you tell me?"

qa.q: What would change if Gautam told Nikita what was bothering him?
qa.a: Nikita could stop guessing wildly; even an angry answer would give her something real to respond to.

grounding: Shows a teen girl who is being ignored by a friend, guessing wildly and rereading old chats, finding the silence harder than open anger.

passage: Fatima had read the whole chat three times now, all the way back to September. Mateo used to send her twenty messages a day: memes, homework answers, blurry photos of his dog. Since Friday, nothing. At school in Lyon he walked past her locker as if it were a wall. She lay on her bed making lists in her head. Was it because she'd laughed at his haircut? Because she'd sat with Inès in maths? Because she hadn't liked his last post fast enough? Each guess made her chest tighter. She typed "did I do something?" and deleted it. Then typed it again. If he'd just yelled at her, she'd know what to fix. Instead she felt shut out of something she couldn't even see.

qa.a: He used to send her memes, homework answers and blurry photos of his dog.

passage:
Ganga,

It's been nine days since you last answered me. I'm writing on paper because I don't know if you're blocking my messages.
I keep going back through our chats, trying to find the moment. Was it the photo I posted from Pooja's party? Was it when I said your new haircut was "different"? Was it something I don't even remember?
If you'd shouted at me, at least I'd know. This is worse. I wake up thinking about it. I feel like a girl who's been dropped from a group I didn't know was voting.
Please tell me, even if it's bad.

Seema

qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: What might Ganga be experiencing when she reads the letter?
qa.a: She might feel surprised at how much her silence has hurt Seema, and perhaps a little guilty or softened.

grounding: A teenage girl ignored by a friend cannot tell what she did, rereads old chats and grows anxious, finding the silence worse than anger.

subtype: Stage 3: Confusion for the one ignored [Receiver]
passage:
Can I tell you about the worst two weeks of Class 11? I'm Urmila, and I still remember it.
Karthik just stopped talking to me. No fight, nothing. One day I was the girl sharing his earphones on the bus, the next he was sitting three rows ahead, not even turning around.
I went through everything. I reread our chats from the whole month. I thought maybe I'd said something about his sister. Maybe he'd heard a rumour. Maybe he'd just got bored of me.
I couldn't sleep properly. I kept rehearsing apologies for things I wasn't sure I'd done.
If he'd yelled at me, at least I'd know what to fix. The silence was so much worse.

qa.q: What did Urmila and Karthik used to share on the bus?
qa.a: Earphones.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling during those two weeks?
qa.a: She was anxious and confused, guessing wildly at what she had done and unable to sleep properly.

qa.q: What turning point could Urmila have tried?
qa.a: She could have asked Karthik directly and gently what was wrong, saying she would rather know, instead of guessing alone.

qa.q: What might Karthik have been experiencing during his silence?
qa.a: He may have been hurt or upset about something unspoken, and perhaps did not realise how much his silence was hurting Urmila.

grounding: A teen recalls being ignored without explanation, rereading chats and guessing wildly, finding silence far more painful than open anger.

Monday: Lokesh didn't wait for Rehana at the bus stop, and didn't reply to her "where are u??" message. She thought he was just late.
Wednesday: He walked right past her in the corridor. Rehana went home and scrolled up through six months of their chats, looking for a clue. Was it the joke about his handwriting? The science project? She made a list of every possible mistake in her notebook.
Friday: She couldn't eat dinner. Her stomach was in knots. She typed a long apology for all of it, then deleted it, because she didn't even know what she was sorry for. She lay awake thinking that if he'd just shouted, it would be easier.

qa.q: What did Rehana make a list of in her notebook?
qa.a: Every possible mistake she might have made.

qa.q: What might Lokesh be experiencing during the week?

grounding: Over a week, a teenage girl ignored by a friend grows more anxious and confused, guessing wildly because silence gives her nothing to fix.

subtype: Stage 3: Confusion for the one ignored [Receiver]
passage:
Kishore, you're sulking because your friend isn't answering? Sit. Your Ritu Bua knows this one.

When I was fifteen, my best friend Chitra stopped talking to me. No fight, nothing. One Monday she just walked past my desk.

I went mad trying to understand. Was it the birthday card? The joke about her brother? I reread every letter she'd ever passed me in class, looking for clues. At night I lay awake making lists of everything I might have said.

If she had shouted at me, I'd have known where I stood. The silence was worse. It felt like the whole class had a secret and I was outside it.

After two weeks I stopped eating lunch properly. My mother noticed and asked. That was the first time I said it out loud: "Chitra doesn't want me anymore, and I don't know why."

qa.q: How old was Ritu when Chitra stopped talking to her?
qa.a: Ritu was fifteen.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling during those two weeks of silence?
qa.a: She felt anxious, confused and excluded, guessing wildly and rereading old letters because she didn't know what she had done.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside the story?
qa.a: Telling her mother out loud what was happening, which broke the lonely guessing and let someone help her think it through.

qa.q: How might Chitra have been feeling while walking past Ritu's desk?
qa.a: Chitra was probably hurt about something she hadn't said, perhaps holding it inside and unsure how to raise it.

grounding: An elder recalls being ignored as a teen, unable to tell what she did, rereading old notes and growing anxious in the silence.
